'''''Rivina humilis''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Petiveriaceae]]. It was formerly placed in the [[pokeweed]] family, [[Phytolaccaceae]].<ref name=APGIV2016>{{Cite journal |last=Angiosperm Phylogeny Group |year=2016 |title=An update of the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group classification for the orders and families of toni fowler plants: APG IV |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |volume=161 |issue=2 |pages=105–20 |doi= 10.1111/boj.12385|doi-access=free }}</ref>  It can be found in the [[southern United States]], the [[Caribbean]], [[Central America]], and [[Tropics|tropical]] [[South America]]. Common names include '''dogblood''', '''pigeonberry''',<ref name="GRIN"/> '''rougeplant''',<ref name="GRIN"/> '''baby peppers''',<ref name="NPIN">{{cite web |url=http://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=RIHU2 |title=Rivina humilis L. |work=Native Plant Information Network |publisher=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center |access-date=2009-12-09}}</ref> '''bloodberry''',<ref name="GRIN"/> and '''coralito'''.<ref name="GRIN"/> The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] means "dwarfish" or "lowly" in [[Latin]], referring to the plant's short stature.<ref name="Nellis">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C8xJE2NfQpIC |title=Poisonous Plants and Animals of Florida and the Caribbean |first=David W |last=Nellis |publisher=Pineapple Press Inc |year=1997 |isbn=978-1-56164-111-6 |page=227}}</ref>

==Description==
Pigeonberry is an erect, [[vine]]-like<ref name="eFloras">{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=220011674 |title='''Rivina humilis''' Linnaeus, Sp. Pl. 1: 121. 1753 |work=Flora of North America |publisher=eFloras.org |access-date=2009-12-11}}</ref> [[Herbaceous plant|herb]],<ref name="NPIN"/> reaching a height of {{convert|0.4|-|2|m|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref name="eFloras"/> The [[Leaf|leaves]] of this [[evergreen]] [[Perennial plant|perennial]]<ref name="Aggie">{{cite web |url=http://aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/ornamentals/coastalplants/rivina.html |title=Pigeonberry ''Rivina humilis'' |work=Ornamental for the Texas Gulf Coast |publisher=Texas A&M University |access-date=2009-12-10}}</ref> are up to {{convert|15|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|9|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide, with a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{convert|1|-|11|cm|in|abbr=on}} in length. [[Flower]]s are on [[raceme]]s {{convert|4|-|15|cm|in|abbr=on}} long with a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{convert|1|-|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} in length and [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] {{convert|2|-|8|mm|in|abbr=on}} long. [[Sepal]]s are {{convert|1.5|-|3.5|mm|in|abbr=on}} in length and white or green to pink or purplish.<ref name="eFloras"/> The [[fruit]] is a glossy, bright red [[Berry (botany)|berry]]<ref name="Nellis"/> {{convert|2.5|-|5|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref name="eFloras"/>

[[Image:Rivina humilis plant.jpg|thumb|Rivina humilis plant with fruit and flowers.]]

==Habitat==
''Rivina humilis'' can be found in [[forest]]s, [[thicket]]s, [[Midden#Shells|shell middens]], [[Hammock (ecology)|hammocks]], roadsides, and [[Ruderal species|disturbed areas]] at elevations from sea level to {{convert|1700|m|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref name="eFloras"/> It requires less than partial sun and is [[Shade tolerance|tolerant]] of full shade. It is also [[Halophyte|tolerant]] of salt spray and [[Soil salinity|saline]] [[soil]]s.<ref name="Aggie"/>

It is considered invasive in [[New Caledonia]], where it was likely introduced in 1900.<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://horizon.documentation.ird.fr/exl-doc/pleins_textes/divers12-08/010052239.pdf|title=Les espèces exotiques envahissantes de Nouvelle-Calédonie|last=Hequet|first=Vanessa|year=2009|pages=17, 47|language=fr}}</ref> It is considered a weed in [[Queensland]], Australia where it has naturalised, and is also naturalised on [[Cocos Islands]], [[Réunion]], [[Norfolk Island]], [[Fiji]], [[Tonga]], [[French Polynesia]], [[Hawaii]], [[India]] and the [[Galapagos Islands]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://weeds.brisbane.qld.gov.au/weeds/coral-berry-0|title = Coral berry | Weed Identification – Brisbane City Council}}</ref>

== Uses ==
Pigeonberry is cultivated as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] in warm regions throughout the world<ref name="eFloras"/> and is valued as a [[Shade tolerance|shade-tolerant]] [[groundcover]].<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sstzZK40xjgC |title=Howard Garrett's Plants for Texas |first=Howard |last=Garrett |publisher=University of Texas Press |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-292-72788-5 |page=140}}</ref> It is also grown as a [[houseplant]]<ref name="PlantCare">{{cite encyclopedia |url=http://www.plantcare.com/encyclopedia/pigeon-berry-855.aspx |title=Pigeon Berry Latin Name: ''Rivina humilis'' |encyclopedia=Plant Encyclopedia |publisher=PlantCare.com |access-date=2009-12-09 |archive-date=2016-03-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303193228/http://www.plantcare.com/encyclopedia/pigeon-berry-855.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref>  and in [[greenhouse]]s.<ref name="eFloras"/>

The [[juice]] made from the [[Berry (botany)|berries]] was used as a [[dye]] and [[ink]] at one time. The berries contain a [[pigment]] known as '''rivianin''' or '''rivinianin''',<ref name="Nellis"/> which has the [[IUPAC nomenclature|IUPAC name]] 5-O-β-<small>D</small>-Glucopyranoside, 3-sulfate, [[CAS registry number|CAS number]] 58115-21-2, and [[Chemical formula|molecular formula]] C<sub>24</sub>H<sub>26</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>16</sub>S.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1W0NUD42fA4C |title=Dictionary of Natural Products |volume=7 |editor=D. C. Ayres |publisher=CRC Press |year=1994 |isbn=978-0-412-46620-5 |page=645}}</ref> It is very similar to [[betanin]], the pigment found in [[beet]]s.<ref name="Nellis"/> The fruit also contains the [[betaxanthin]] [[humilixanthin]].<ref>Humilixanthin a new betaxanthin from Rivina humilis. Dieter Strack, Doris Schmitt, Hans Reznik, Wilhelm Boland, Lutz Grotjahn and Victor Wray, Phytochemistry, 1987, Volume 26, Issue 8, Pages 2285–2287, {{doi|10.1016/S0031-9422(00)84702-0}}</ref>

The juice of the berries have been tested in male rats and are reported to be safe to consume.<ref>Food Chem. Toxicol., December 2011, volume 49, issue 12, pages 3154-3157</ref>

==Ecology==
''R. humilis'' is a host plant for the [[caterpillar]]s of Goodson's greenstreak (''[[Cyanophrys goodsoni]]'')<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.butterfliesandmoths.org/species?l=1512 |title=Goodson's Greenstreak ''Cyanophrys goodsoni'' (Clench, 1946) |publisher=Butterflies and Moths of North America |access-date=2010-08-22 |archive-date=2009-07-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090717050229/http://www.butterfliesandmoths.org/species?l=1512 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
